solutions.latex:
$$2e^{-x}=e^x-1\Rightarrow\dfrac{2}{e^x}=e^x-1\Rightarrow 2=e^{2x}-e^x\Rightarrow e^{2x}-e^x-2=0$$

Let $m=e^x$: $m^2-m-2=0$, $(m-2)(m+1)=0$.

$e^x=2$ or $e^x=-1$, but $e^x\neq -1$. So $x=\ln 2$.

When $x=\ln 2$: $y=2e^{-\ln 2}=2\times\dfrac{1}{2}=1$.

So the curves intersect at $(\ln 2,1)$.

solutions.latex:
The area under the curve is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}bh=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 0.5=1\ \text{unit}^2$.

So $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx=1$ and $f(x)=0$ outside $(0,4)$, so $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$. So it could be a continuous probability density function.

If $0\le x<2$: $m=\dfrac{0.5}{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}$, $y$-intercept $0$, so $y=\dfrac{x}{4}$.

If $2\le x\le 4$: $m=\dfrac{-0.5}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{4}$; when $x=4$, $y=0$: $y-0=-\dfrac{1}{4}(x-4)$, so $y=1-\dfrac{x}{4}$.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{4} & 0\le x<2\\ 1-\dfrac{x}{4} & 2\le x\le 4\\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

solutions.latex:
The particle stops or turns when $v=0$: $1-2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}=0$, so $\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\dfrac{\pi t}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3},\dfrac{7\pi}{3}$, so $t=1,5,7$ seconds.

In the first 4 seconds the particle changes direction at $t=1$, so calculate $t=0$ to $t=1$ and $t=1$ to $t=4$ separately.

$$d=\left|\int_0^1\left(1-2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right)dt\right|+\left|\int_1^4\left(1-2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right)dt\right|=\left|\left[t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right]_0^1\right|+\left|\left[t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right]_1^4\right|$$

$$=\left|1-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right|+\left|\left(4+\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\left(1-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right|=\left|1-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right|+\left|3+\dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right|$$

$$=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi}-1+3+\dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi}=2+\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi}$$

So the exact distance is $\left(2+\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right)$ m.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: finding the endpoints of motion; 1: allowing for change of direction of particle and setting up appropriate sum of areas; 1: finding the exact distance
1: differentiating and finding acceleration; 1: exact value at $t=4$

solutions.latex:
Stationary points: $f'(x)=6x^2-4x^3=0$, so $2x^2(3-2x)=0$, $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$. When $x=0$, $y=0$; when $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$, $y=\dfrac{27}{16}$. So the stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{27}{16}\right)$.

Nature:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & -1 & 0 & 1 & \frac{3}{2} & 2\\ \hline f'(x) & 10 & 0 & 2 & 0 & -8\\ & \text{slope } / & - & / & - & \backslash \end{array}$$

So $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion and $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{27}{16}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.

Inflexion: $f''(x)=12x-12x^2=0$, so $12x(1-x)=0$, $x=0$ or $x=1$.

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & \frac{1}{2} & 1 & 2\\ \hline f''(x) & 3 & 0 & -24 \end{array}$$

Concavity changes, so when $x=1$, $y=1$: $(1,1)$ is a point of inflexion, and $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion (from the nature table).
